name: Gareth Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Gareth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and this is all confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sales negotiator at the Brookfield branch of Hallmark Homes, a franchise, out in a commuter town about forty minutes from the city. I'm in at nine for the morning meeting, where the manager, Steve, reads out everyone's numbers. Then it's calls, chasing offers, and three or four viewings in the afternoon, mostly three-bed semis. I drive a branded car with the logo on the side, which my mates never let me forget.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is getting an offer accepted and ringing a young couple to tell them. You can hear them screaming down the phone. The hard bit is that my pay is mostly commission and the base is low, so a slow month really hurts. My girlfriend Amy is a dental nurse and we're trying to save for a deposit, but we've got under a month put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool, not the end of the world. I'd probably make a joke in the office group chat about the robots not taking over after all. People would laugh and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the job stays roughly as it is, which is fine. The pressure is still the commission and the market, not AI. If rates go up again, viewings drop and so does my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and try to pick up a few more listings. I'd ask Steve if the time saved on paperwork could go into more valuations, because that's where the money is. And I'd keep putting a hundred a month into the deposit pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time AI saves you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More valuations, ideally. If I win the listing, I get a better cut when it sells. Writing the brochure was always the boring bit anyway, so if the computer does it, good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned saving for a deposit. How's that going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. We've got about three weeks of money in the bank and the deposit pot is a joke right now. My girlfriend Amy says we'll get there by thirty, I say thirty-two.

I'd joke in the office chat that the **robots** didn't take over.
think: The job stays **roughly the same**, which suits me.
My real pressure is **commission** and the housing market, not AI.
do: Ask Steve to turn saved paperwork time into **more valuations**.
Keep putting **a hundred** a month into the house deposit pot.

fieldNote: Gareth's worries are **commission swings** and interest rates, not technology.

steps.text: Ask manager Steve to swap paperwork time for more valuations
Put a hundred a month into the house deposit pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and we've had change before. I'd say good agents will be fine, it's the lazy ones who should worry. That's what you say in front of the manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not sure I'm one of the good ones. I'm average. If head office gives every branch an AI that does listings, chasing and booking, they'll want fewer negotiators doing more viewings each. I could be the one they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools more once I saw the top sellers doing well with them, probably within a few months. I'd keep saving, and I'd ask Steve what the branch plan is. I'd also update my CV quietly, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hallmark is a franchise. What would head office do here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roll out one system to every office, set new targets, and tell us we're freed up for the human side. Then six months later the numbers show fewer of us can do the same work. I've seen it happen with the old call centre they used for leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using the tools more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I'd seen it work for someone else. My colleague Lauren already uses it for her follow-up emails and she's well ahead of me this quarter. I'd ask her to show me.

I'd frame it as normal **change** in front of the manager.

do: Learn the **AI tools** within months, starting with Lauren's follow-up emails.
Update my **CV** quietly while still saving for the deposit.
feel: He feels **anxious**, but not yet panicking.

fieldNote: There's a clear gap between his **public confidence** and private doubt.
He waits for proof from a **top seller** before adopting tools.
He expects **franchise-wide targets** to cut staff over time.

steps.text: Ask colleague Lauren to show him her AI follow-up emails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're all in the same boat and the government needs to sort it. I'd probably keep quiet online, because I don't know what the answer is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone within a year or two. The negotiating, the chasing, the valuation reports, an AI does all that better and cheaper. Hallmark would keep a handful of people for keys and viewings, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the branded car back early and stop the deposit saving so we have a cushion for rent. I'd look for work in something hands-on, maybe with Amy's brother who fits kitchens. Every spare pound would go into a rainy-day fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the deposit plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put it on hold, that's the honest answer. Amy would be gutted, but you can't buy a house when you don't know if you'll have a job. That's the conversation I'd dread most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come three years after the thinking AI. Does that help with viewings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but not much. Viewings are the only hands-on bit and a buyer can walk round a semi on their own with a video call. Kitchen fitting gets the full three years, which is why I'd look at that.

say: I'd say we're all in the **same boat** and the government must sort it.
I'd keep quiet **online**, because I don't know the answer.
think: My job would be **gone** within a year or two.
AI does **negotiating and valuations** better and cheaper than me.
do: Pause the **deposit saving** and build a rent cushion instead.
Look for **kitchen fitting** work with Amy's brother, which gets three more years.
feel: He feels **alarmed**, like the floor has dropped.
S2.quote: You can't buy a house when you don't know if you'll have a job.
fieldNote: The **house deposit** is the first casualty, and telling Amy is what he dreads.
He picks **kitchen fitting** because hands-on work gets three more years.
He sees **viewings** as barely protected by the robot gap.

steps.text: Put the house purchase with Amy on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have some time and should use it. I'd tell the lads at five-a-side to think about trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have a couple of good years in sales, then it's over. If I'm smart, I'd use those years to get a trade sorted. If I'm not, I'll be thirty-two with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd learn the AI tools to keep my numbers up while it lasts. Then I'd start a part-time kitchen fitting course, or help Amy's brother on Saturdays. We'd keep the deposit going but smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I feel I could handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first year look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools to hit my numbers, and spend weekends learning kitchens. Basically two jobs for a while. Amy would see less of me, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Steve say if you told him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say good for you, and probably mean it, because he'd be worried about his own job. Branch managers do a lot of reports and targets, and that's exactly what AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, let's get on with it. I'd still want the government to have a plan for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay. I'd buy the house, do some years in sales, and learn a trade in my thirties. The risk is getting comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling and saving for the deposit, and learn the AI tools as they come. In a few years I'd start a trade course part-time. I'd try to pay off the car finance early too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a bit of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that change the deposit plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still buy, maybe in a couple of years. That's the version where Amy and I get our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk with all that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting lazy. If the money is good for a few years, I'd think it'll last forever. It won't.

Start a part-time **trade course** in a few years and clear the car finance.

S4.quote: If the money is good for a few years, I'd think it'll last forever. It won't.
fieldNote: With ten years, the **house purchase** with Amy survives.
He names **complacency** as his main risk.
He still expects to leave **estate agency** eventually, even in the slowest picture.

steps.text: Keep saving for the house deposit with Amy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Amy and I would lose the house plan and I'd have nothing to fall back on. What would help is cheap trade courses you can do while working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the buyers. If agents go, first-time buyers lose the person who fights their corner on price.

headlineQuote: If agents go, first-time buyers lose the person who fights their corner on price.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** sales negotiator at a franchise branch in a commuter town.
He lives with Amy, a **dental nurse**, and they're saving for a house deposit.
He's **pragmatic**, adopts tools once proven, and admits he's average.
His mood rises from **uneasy** to alarmed as AGI comes faster.
He'd move into **kitchen fitting**, which gets three extra years before robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because the house plan would collapse.
